_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- STATE discovery response deadlines.
Phase 5 item 3. Michigan and Pennsylvania only, and the reason Ohio and
Indiana are absent is the main finding of this item.
THE FINDING: HALF OF THESE STATES DO NOT SET A DISCOVERY DEADLINE AT ALL.
Item 3 was scoped as 'state discovery equivalents for OH/IN/MI/PA, reusing
the verified computation standards'. Reading the four states' actual rule
text shows they do not have equivalents -- two of them are a structurally
different kind of provision:
Ohio Civ.R. 33(A):   'within a period designated by the party submitting
the interrogatories, NOT LESS THAN twenty-eight days
after the service of the interrogatories'
Ohio Civ.R. 36(A)(1): 'within a period designated in the request, NOT LESS
THAN twenty-eight days after service'
Ind. T.R. 33(C):     'within a period designated by the party submitting
the interrogatories, NOT LESS THAN thirty days'
Ind. T.R. 36(A):     'within a period designated in the request, NOT LESS
THAN thirty days after service thereof'
In all four, the operative deadline is whatever the PROPOUNDING PARTY
designated in the request. The rule supplies only a FLOOR on what may be
designated. Twenty-eight and thirty are therefore not deadlines -- they are
the minimum a valid request may demand.
SO THEY ARE NOT SEEDED. Encoding Ohio as a 28-day rule would put a date on
screen that is not the user's deadline whenever the request designated
longer, which is most of the time. The error direction is 'safe' (too
early), but Phase 4's decision gate established that a TRUE statement that
invites a WRONG INFERENCE is its own failure mode, and this is exactly that
shape. It is the same call already made for Mich. Ct. R. 2.108(A)(3) in
Phase 3 (a floor on judicial discretion, refused) and for Rule 56 response
deadlines in Phase 5 item 2 (set by local rule, refused). The engine has no
field for the period a propounding party designated, and inventing one
would be inventing a case fact.
WHAT WOULD FIX IT, named rather than silently deferred: a rule shape that
takes the designated period as a required INPUT and validates it against
the rule's floor -- refusing when a request designates fewer days than the
rule permits, which is itself a real and useful check. That is a genuine
engine capability, not a seed, and belongs in its own phase with its own
tests. Until it exists, Ohio and Indiana discovery deadlines refuse with
NO_MATCHING_RULE, and the coverage card shows they are absent.
WHAT IS SEEDED, because Michigan and Pennsylvania really do set fixed
periods. Every value read from primary source 2026-08-22 and quoted.
MICHIGAN HAS A SECOND, DEFENDANT-SPECIFIC PERIOD in both rules -- a
defendant may answer within 42 days after being served with the summons and
complaint, rather than 28 days after the discovery request. That is a
genuinely different trigger EVENT (service of process, not service of the
request), so each is its own rule with its own trigger, the same treatment
MCR 2.108(A)'s 21/28 split already gets. The engine must never guess which
applies, and a defendant early in a case can have both running.
PENNSYLVANIA RULE 4014(b) CARRIES A FLOOR TOO, and only the fixed part is
encoded: the 30-day response period is a real deadline and is seeded, while
'a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before
the expiration of forty-five days after service of the original process' is
a floor on what can be demanded of a defendant, not a deadline, and is
disclosed in the rule's note rather than encoded as a second rule.
NO SERVICE EXTENSION IS ATTACHED TO ANY RULE HERE. Michigan handles
manner-of-service by giving a different PERIOD rather than adding days (the
same finding as Phase 3's MCR 2.108(A)(2)), and Pennsylvania has no
automatic mail extension at all (Phase 3 finding 6 -- Pa.R.C.P. 440 adds no
days and Rule 248 is court-granted). Attaching FRCP 6(d) to a state rule
would import a federal provision that does not govern.
PRODUCTION-OF-DOCUMENTS RULES ARE NOT IN THIS FILE. Mich. Ct. R. 2.310 and
Pa.R.C.P. 4009.12 were not read to the same standard as the rules above and
are not encoded from inference. They are a straightforward addition once
read directly -- absence here means not yet verified, not verified absent.

authority.quote: serve the answers and objections, if any, on all other parties within 28 days after the interrogatories are served
authority.note: A FIXED period, unlike Ohio Civ.R. 33(A) and Ind. T.R. 33(C), which set only a floor on what the propounding party may designate and are therefore not seeded at all -- see this file's readme. The separate 42-day defendant period runs from service of the summons and complaint, a different trigger event, and is its own rule here. No service_extension: Michigan handles manner of service by setting a different period rather than adding days, and importing FRCP 6(d) into a state rule would apply a provision that does not govern.

rules.label: Answers to interrogatories by a defendant, counted from service of process (Michigan)

authority.quote: a defendant may serve answers within 42 days after being served with the summons and complaint
authority.note: The rule says a defendant MAY use this period, so early in a case a defendant can have both this and the 28-day period from the request running, and the later of the two is the one that matters to them. The engine computes whichever is asked for and does not choose between them -- the trigger names are deliberately distinct, and the trigger here is service of PROCESS, not service of the discovery request. The trigger name is suffixed _for_discovery to keep it distinct from the answer-to-complaint rule that already uses service of process in this jurisdiction, since two rules sharing one trigger name would be refused as AMBIGUOUS_RULE.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission (Michigan — unanswered matters are ADMITTED)

authority.quote: within 28 days after service of the request, or within a shorter or longer time as the court may allow
authority.note: As with the federal Rule 36(a)(3), the consequence of missing this is substantive and automatic -- a matter to which no proper response is served is DEEMED ADMITTED, with no motion required by the requesting party. Carried in the rule label for that reason. The separate 42-day defendant period runs from service of process and is its own rule. Expressly variable by court order, quoted above.

rules.label: Answer to a request for admission by a defendant, counted from service of process (Michigan)

authority.quote: Unless the court orders a shorter time a defendant may serve an answer or objection within 42 days after being served with the summons and complaint.
authority.note: Distinct trigger from the 28-day period, and distinct from the interrogatory 42-day rule, because three separate deadlines in this jurisdiction can otherwise run from service of process and the engine refuses AMBIGUOUS_RULE rather than choosing among rules sharing one trigger name.

rules.label: Answers and objections to written interrogatories (Pennsylvania)

authority.quote: serve a copy of the answers, and objections if any, within thirty days after the service of the interrogatories
authority.note: A genuinely fixed period with NO separate defendant provision, unlike Michigan's rules and unlike Pennsylvania's own Rule 4014(b). No service_extension: Pennsylvania has no automatic mail extension at all -- Pa.R.C.P. 440 adds no days and Rule 248 is a court-granted extension, established in Phase 3 finding 6. effective_from is 2024-01-01 for the same reason as every other Pennsylvania rule here: that is when Pa.R.J.A. 107 took effect and Pa.R.C.P. 106 was rescinded, and this row is the pairing of the count with a computation standard.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission (Pennsylvania — unanswered matters are ADMITTED)

authority.quote: The matter is admitted unless, within thirty days after service of the request, or within such shorter or longer time as the court may allow, the party to whom the request is directed serves upon the party requesting the admission an answer verified by the party or an objection
authority.note: ONLY THE FIXED PART IS ENCODED. The same rule continues: 'unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of forty-five days after service of the original process upon him or her.' That is a FLOOR protecting a defendant, not a deadline -- it states the earliest a defendant can be required to answer, not when they must. It is disclosed here rather than encoded as a second rule, the same treatment given to Ohio's and Indiana's designated-period floors, which is why those states have no discovery rules in this file at all. A defendant served with admissions early in a case should check this floor by hand. Unanswered matters are ADMITTED by operation of the rule, carried in the label.
